notes.5: The least able candidates overall tended to choose Distractor D using only the group numbers rather than interpreting the likely charge on the ions and deducing the formula of the compound. For these questions it can be helpful to use the Periodic Table provided to identify each element to check whether the answer appears correct.
notes.6: This question was not well answered. The most common response was Distractor D. Candidates are reminded that intermolecular forces exist between molecules. The word molecule is used to describe a substance that has a simple covalent structure and not ionic or metallic.
notes.8: Over a third of candidates calculated the ratio of percentages rather than the ratio of moles and chose Distractor D.
notes.9: This was a demanding question. Most candidates incorrectly assumed that the reactants reacted in a 1 : 1 ratio and chose Distractor B.
notes.13: This question discriminated well between the most and least able candidates. The least able candidates were more likely to choose any of the other options equally rather than the correct answer.
notes.15: Distractor A was the most common incorrect answer. Although the collision rate between reacting particles will increase when concentration increases, the concentration has no effect on the energy of each particle.
notes.17: Questions about the oxidising agent and the reducing agent always require the reactants to be chosen rather than the products. Many candidates chose Distractor C or Distractor D which only showed the products of the reaction.
notes.18: Although most of the stronger candidates answered this question correctly, the weaker candidates were more likely to choose any one of the distractors, especially Distractor B. This suggests that candidates recognise that uncombined elements have an oxidation number of zero but find the determination of oxidation numbers within compounds more difficult.
notes.19: This question was not well answered. The equation shows ammonia, NH , accepting H+ to become NH + 3 4 which is the behaviour of a base. Over two thirds of the candidates thought that ammonia is acidic and chose Distractor A or Distractor B.
notes.25: This question was less well answered than anticipated. It was assumed that most candidates would recall the order of reactivity of metals. Although the correct answer was favoured overall, all the distractors were commonly chosen.
notes.26: Similarly to Question 6, many candidates confused the term ‘intermolecular forces’ with a bond type. When describing the difference between alloys and pure metals, the size and movement of particles is essential information. �PAGE�16
notes.32: Weaker candidates appeared to be guessing in this question. Candidates are advised to be cautious when answering questions which include the word ‘not’.
notes.37: Candidates should take care when reading chemical names which are similar to other chemical names. In this question, propane was confused with propene and so many candidates chose Distractor C. The other common error was to confuse the amide bond in nylon with an ester bond. Distractor B was also chosen by many candidates. �PAGE�17
notes.general_comments:
Candidates found this to be an accessible paper overall with many questions showing good discrimination
between candidates. For several questions the weaker candidates appear to have been guessing which
suggests that the core tier may have been more appropriate. The average mark was slightly higher than last
year. Overall candidates found Question 4, 22, 30, 31, 33 and 39 to have the least challenge.
Question 6, 9, 17, 19, 25 and 37 were most demanding.
Questions on oxidation and reduction were particularly poorly answered by the weakest candidates overall.
Many candidates found questions involving numbers or a calculation demanding.
Questions on the reactions of acids and metals were less well answered than in previous series.
